analysis.one_liner: Lets workers and consumers sue in court instead of being forced into private arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote, dying in a House committee after being referred to a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies routinely require workers and customers to sign away their right to sue before a dispute even happens, forcing them into private arbitration instead. This bill would make such pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, restoring access to the courts and to class actions. Courts, not arbitrators, would decide whether an arbitration agreement is valid.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with discrimination, wage, or harassment claims, and consumers with complaints about products, credit, or services, who currently must take those disputes to private arbitrators with no appeal and often alone. It also restores the ability to join class actions, the main practical way to challenge small-dollar harms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers with legal claims

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar any pre-dispute arbitration agreement from being valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of an employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights dispute.

It would restore access to court and to class actions, because its antitrust definition covers disputes where plaintiffs seek class certification, and because forced arbitration clauses typically also block class lawsuits.
It would have courts, not arbitrators, decide whether an arbitration agreement applies, making challenges to abusive contract terms a matter of public, reviewable law.

It preserves voluntary arbitration agreed to after a dispute arises, and leaves union contract arbitration intact except that arbitration cannot waive an employee's right to go to court over statutory or constitutional rights.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that embed mandatory arbitration clauses in employment contracts and consumer terms, especially large financial firms, employers, and sellers of goods and services, which would face courtroom litigation and class actions they currently avoid.

drawbacks.text: Companies argue arbitration is faster and cheaper for both sides, and that the bill could push more small claims into costly litigation rather than resolve them quickly; the bill itself acknowledges arbitration is acceptable when truly voluntary, occurring after a dispute arises.

The bill's effectiveness would depend on courts policing the boundary between pre-dispute clauses (banned) and post-dispute agreements (allowed), and it does nothing for people whose existing arbitration contracts remain in force, since it applies only to disputes arising after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: it gives workers and consumers back the practical ability to enforce rights against companies with far more bargaining power, and it restores class actions for small-dollar harms where individual lawsuits make no economic sense. The cost falls on companies as litigation exposure, and some disputes may take longer or cost more than arbitration would have. The strongest honest objection is that mandatory arbitration can be quicker and cheaper in routine cases, but that advantage is bought by forfeiting the appeal, precedent, and public accountability that courts provide.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Hank Johnson introduced the bill on March 7, 2017, with 45 original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On March 17, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.

The bill attracted 82 Democratic cosponsors but no recorded action beyond those referrals, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that keep mandatory arbitration clauses in employment and consumer contracts, because they continue to resolve disputes in private arbitration instead of court.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 45 original cosponsors.

for.name: 82 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on referral but never brought it to a markup or a vote in the two years it held it.

sides.party_line_note: All 82 cosponsors were Democrats, all original sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the Judiciary Committee, chaired by a Republican, never acted on it.

industries.industry: Financial services and credit card companies
industries.note: Banks and card issuers put mandatory arbitration clauses in the fine print of accounts, credit cards, and loans. The bill would let customers take disputes to court and join class actions, the remedy most useful for small-dollar overcharges affecting millions of customers at once.
Many employers require workers to sign away court access for discrimination, wage, and harassment claims as a condition of the job. The bill would restore workers' right to sue in court.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Retailers, telecoms, and online services embed arbitration clauses in consumer terms of service. The bill would expose them to lawsuits and class actions over products and billing practices they currently shield from court.
